## What interactmeta adds

Contribution-adjusted meta-analysis (CAMS) is a model for
treatment-by-subgroup interactions from subgroup-level aggregate data
(Panaro, Röver & Friede 2025): [*Consistent Bayesian meta-analysis on
subgroup specific effects and
interactions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18785).

The work the package does is this map:

$$
(y_{Aj},y_{Bj})
\;\rightarrow\;
(m_j,g_j,\pi_j)
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{overall and interaction blocks}
\;\rightarrow\;
\{\gamma,\;\mu_A(\pi),\;\mu_B(\pi),\;M(\pi)\}.
$$

`bayesmeta` and `metafor` can be used to fit the two blocks, but they
do not construct $\pi_j$, rotate the observations, reconstruct
subgroup estimands, or guarantee $\mu_B(\pi)-\mu_A(\pi)=\gamma$ by
design. This additional machinery is what `cams()` provides. In this
context, Difference of Averages (DA) and Average Difference (AD) are
distinct constructions (Panaro, Röver & Friede, 2026) and should not
be conflated with CAMS; see
[`vignette("consistent-interactions")`](consistent-interactions.html).

```{r load}
library(interactmeta)
```

## Subgroup-level inputs

Each row represents one subgroup within one trial. `yi` is the observed
effect on the **log** scale (here, the log incidence-rate ratio
(IRR)), and `vi` is its sampling variance.

```{r data}
age_es <- escalc(measure = "IRR", yi = yi, vi = vi, data = age)
head(age_es)
```

## Information fraction and orthogonal summaries

For a trial that reports subgroups $A$ (reference) and $B$,

$$
\pi_j = \frac{1/\sigma_{Bj}^2}{1/\sigma_{Aj}^2 + 1/\sigma_{Bj}^2}.
$$

This $\pi_j$ is an **information fraction (IF)**: the proportion of a
trial's total precision contributed by subgroup $B$. It is not a
survey share or a target-population mixing proportion. Using the
same observed subgroup effects, CAMS defines two coordinates: the
within-trial contrast and the IF-weighted combined-population effect,

$$
g_j = y_{Bj}-y_{Aj},\qquad
m_j = (1-\pi_j)y_{Aj}+\pi_j y_{Bj}.
$$

With independent subgroup sampling errors
($\mathrm{Cov}(y_{Aj},y_{Bj})=0$), one has
$\mathrm{Var}(g_j)=\sigma_{Aj}^2+\sigma_{Bj}^2$, and
$\mathrm{Cov}(g_j,m_j)=0$ if and only if $\pi_j$ is chosen as this
information fraction. Under normality, this orthogonality implies that the
sampling model factorizes into an overall block in $m_j$ and an interaction
block in $g_j$. That zero within-trial covariance is the assumption used by
`cams()` today. If the covariance were known and nonzero, a different IF
(and different $\mathrm{Var}(g_j)$, $\mathrm{Var}(m_j)$) would be needed to
keep the blocks orthogonal; that path is not implemented in this package.

```{r ifrac}
age_if <- ifrac(age_es, reference = "Younger")
```

```{r ifrac-head}
head(age_if)
```

## Fit the two blocks

The overall series in $m_j$ and the interaction series in $g_j$ are
fitted as independent blocks, after which the CAMS estimands are
reconstructed. Inference may be Bayesian or frequentist; that choice
is considered only after establishing the identities below. In the
Bayesian case, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is not inherently
required for random-effects meta-analysis (Röver, 2020).

Package Bayesian defaults match bayesmeta on heterogeneity (improper
uniform on $\tau$) with $N(0,10)$ on fixed effects. Here we set the
weakly informative / empirical half-normal scales from Panaro, Röver &
Friede (arXiv:2606.23968) explicitly: HN(0.5) on overall heterogeneity
and HN(0.1) on interaction heterogeneity (interaction $\tau$ is typically
smaller).

```{r fit, cache = TRUE}
fit <- cams(
  age_es,
  reference = "Younger",
  tau.prior = function(tau) bayesmeta::dhalfnormal(tau, scale = 0.5),
  tau.interaction.prior = function(tau) bayesmeta::dhalfnormal(tau, scale = 0.1)
)
```

```{r fit-print}
fit
```

## Identities the model preserves

Stored `b_Intercept` is $\alpha$ and stored `b_subgroup*` is the interaction $\gamma$. Stored `b_ifrac` is the common subgroup slope $\beta_{\mathrm{pkg}}=\theta-\gamma$, not the slope of the combined-population line. Then

\begin{align}
\mu_A(\pi)&=\alpha+\pi b_{\mathrm{ifrac}},\\
\mu_B(\pi)&=\alpha+\pi b_{\mathrm{ifrac}}+\gamma,\\
M(\pi)&=\alpha+\pi(b_{\mathrm{ifrac}}+\gamma),
\end{align}

and the two identities that make CAMS a contribution-adjusted model rather than two independent subgroup meta-analyses:

$$
\mu_B(\pi)-\mu_A(\pi)=\gamma,
\qquad
M(\pi)=(1-\pi)\mu_A(\pi)+\pi\mu_B(\pi).
$$

The subgroup lines are parallel with gap $\gamma$. $M(\pi)$ is its own linear predictor, not the average of the two subgroup median curves. Intervals for $M(\pi)$ keep the joint $(\alpha,\theta)$ structure of the overall block.

## Estimands at a reporting $\pi$

By default, the reporting extractors evaluate estimands at the **reporting information fraction** \(\widetilde{\pi}\). `type = "Pooled"` returns the fixed-effect linear predictor evaluated at that \(\pi\), whereas `type = "Prediction"` additionally incorporates a new-trial random effect. The model itself is fitted on the log scale; use `exponentiate = TRUE` only when ratio-scale results are desired for reporting.

```{r estimands-interactions}
interactions(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

```{r estimands-subgroups}
subgroups(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

```{r estimands-combined}
combined(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

`overall()` is an alias of `combined()`. A scalar `contribution` is a plug-in $\pi$; leaving it `NULL` mixes the posterior of $\widetilde{\pi}$.

```{r plug-in}
subgroups(fit, contribution = 0.5, type = "Pooled", exponentiate = TRUE)
```

## Forest plot

The forest draws the observed subgroup table with **Pooled** and **Prediction** diamonds. The IF column is each row's share of that trial's precision. Default `type = "subgroups"` is the two subgroup blocks. Use `type = "interaction"` or `type = "overall"` for those CAMS blocks.

```{r forest, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

## Effects across $\pi$

The contribution plot is the CAMS meta-regression: $\mu_A(\pi)$, $\mu_B(\pi)$, and $M(\pi)$ over the observed information-fraction range. Study points sit at each trial's own $\pi_j$.

```{r contribution, fig.height = 5}
plot_contribution(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

## Bayesian or frequentist inference

CAMS can be fitted using Bayesian or frequentist inference. These are
not two different models. Bayesian inference is implemented using the
bayesmeta / discrete approximation of a mixture distribution via
restricted divergence (DIRECT) quadrature approach (the default;
Röver and Friede 2017). Frequentist inference is implemented using
the metafor approach (restricted maximum likelihood, REML, or
maximum likelihood, ML). Extractors return the same CAMS quantities
in either case; credible intervals come from the DIRECT mixture, and
confidence intervals from the `rma` covariance. Default pooled
diamonds mix \(\omega(\tau)\) on the DIRECT support (Bayesian) or
plug in \(\omega(\tau)\) (frequentist). See
`vignette("engine-comparison")`. Remaining extractors, plots, and
the posterior workflow are `vignette("further")`.
